project_workflows.title: ADU exterior wall fabrication package (LOD 400 + BOM)
project_workflows.intent: Turn the exterior walls of a one-storey wood-frame ADU into prefabricated wall panels: 2x6 framing, 3/4in plywood, bevel siding, XPS cavity fill; one assembly per wall; shop drawings; BOM and cost.

steps.do: Build and flex-test component families (lumber, sheet panel, insulation block, siding board)
Write the layout rule (studs 16in o.c., 3-stud corners, double top plate lapped, openings with king/jack/header/sill/cripples, sheets on stud centres, siding courses, foam per cavity)
2D preview from the rule: studs in plan, sheet and board joints in elevations; user confirms or corrects the rule
Resolve design conflicts found by the preview as user decisions (door lowered to fit a header) and re-preview
Replay the rule in 3D per wall; disallow joins on all framing; verify every piece; group into assemblies
Assembly shop drawings: framing and sheathing elevations, plan section, 3D, part list; trade dimension style; PDF review
Quantities and cost from the model; governed BOM parameters
Issue: one shop drawing sheet per panel that differs (identical panels once, with a quantity), add every assembly sheet to the print set, export the set to PDF, open the PDF and check each sheet
Synchronize with central after the package passes its checks, with a comment; on cloud models save local before and after (operating rule in AGENTS.md)

project_workflows.title: ADU shed roof assembly (LOD 400 + BOM): framing, deck, standing seam, trim, insulation
project_workflows.intent: Replace a placeholder shed roof with a real build-up and turn it into one roof assembly: 2x8 rafters @ 24in, walls rebuilt to fit the roof (taller high wall, raked end walls), frieze blocks, outlookers and fly rafters, 3/4in plywood deck, standing seam roofing, 1x10 fascia and barge boards covering every exposed rafter cut, batts and drywall inside the wall lines, shop drawing and BOM with cost.

steps.do: Read the roof as modelled before planning: type, slope, footprint, overhangs, height gap between flat wall plates and the sloped roof underside, neighbouring elements (e.g. a trellis under the eave)

Ask the decisions that belong to the user: structure (rafters on walls built to fit the roof vs trusses), member size (engineer flag), roofing for the slope (5 deg excludes asphalt shingles), overhangs, trim, soffit, insulation, assembly grouping
2D preview from the layout rule: framing plan, sheathing plan, section; check every view direction; look at the exported images

Replace the placeholder roof: new footprint roof with the real layers (Revit 2024 cannot edit roof sketches or attach walls by API), user re-attaches the walls, then delete the old roof; guard every transaction
Component families: lumber types 2x8 / 2x4 flat; work-plane-based copies of sheet and insulation families; flex-test the plane orientation

Build from one layout rule in a dry run with an all-pairs clash check; offset square-cut ends by depth x sin(slope); commit only with allow-listed contacts; trim must cover every exposed cut; insulation only inside the exterior wall lines
Create the assembly after Regenerate; name it after commit
BOM from the model: check every piece against its stock size; reset Cost and Type Comments on duplicated types; price with source and date; stock conversion, waste, tax, range
Shop drawing: framing plan with deck hidden, deck layout, section along the slope, 3D, parts list, dimensions one per transaction, BOM note; export and look at the sheet

project_workflows.title: Weekly BIM coordination of a federated cloud project: collect, check, correct, report, archive
project_workflows.intent: Keep a federated cloud project current in one weekly session: collect model data in an unattended batch, add LOIN completeness and a clash run, check everything against fixed rules and last week's snapshot, repair what is safe to repair, queue the rest for approval, and publish one dashboard report with recommendations for the team.

steps.do: Preflight: Revit idle at Home with no model open (ask before closing the user's work), bridge alive, disk and collaboration cache space, registry compared with the cloud folder (new or renamed models), report folder REPORTS/<date> created

Collect in batch (unattended): Model Health Check and PBP + Worksets report over all registry models, then Export Schedules (instance parameters, project information, sheet list); output folder typed explicitly

Collect deep, read-only: shared position at the internal origin per model against the authority, link instances per host with workset and total transform (links loaded, not from the batch report), Project Information keys, standard schedules present
LOIN snapshot: from the exported instance-parameter schedules count filled values per model, category and field (family elements only); score against the client's LOIN table, or state the assumption

Clash run: open the discipline models in one session (link worksets closed), intersect the agreed category pairs, separate penetrations, group clashes, owner by routing priority; close the models unsaved. Use the cloud clash service instead where the project has one
Check: one dataset per source (models, links, warnings, LOIN, clashes) keyed by model or pair and week; findings per model and rule; week-over-week deltas from the second week on

Correct: safe fixes automatically (repair links to the matrix, missing building name, missing standard schedules, then sync); anything that moves geometry, changes coordinates or deletes waits for the coordinator's approval

Report: one dashboard page in the fixed report form (headline, tiles, recommendations, clashes, LOIN, warnings, checks, link matrix, model contents, not collected); every number drawn from the datasets, none typed

Print: one PDF booklet per model in the same unattended batch (ACC Gate 'Print PDFs from Print Intel workbooks'); set-up once per model: fixed print set, Print Intel workbook, PrintJobs row; check page counts against the sets and run the drift check when sheets change
Archive: keep raw outputs in REPORTS/<date>; append the week's datasets to history; submit new lessons to the ARPL inbox (Revit and ZEN alike)

packs.title: Assembly naming and identical panels

environment.tool: RevitBridge 0.4.0 (local Revit API bridge, MCP) with run_csharp

use_when: creating and naming Revit assemblies
several identical panels or modules need drawings
packs.rule: Name assemblies after commit; document identical assemblies once with a quantity ('build 2'). Identical panels may share one assembly type only while their geometry stays identical. When they diverge (raked end walls are mirror images, not copies), give each its own type before editing members: changing the members of one instance of a shared type opens a modal Revit dialog no script can answer and copies the change to the other instances (FP15). An assembly made with AssemblyInstance.Create gets a frame along the project axes; set it with SetTransform (BasisX along the wall, BasisY to the interior) before creating its views (FP16).
validation: Assembly type names and member counts read back

packs.title: Device placement follows the framing (manufacturer's standpoint)

environment.tool: RevitBridge 0.4.0 with run_csharp

use_when: placing receptacles, switches, lights, smoke alarms, floor boxes or other devices in framed walls, roofs or floors
layout previews for prefab wall, roof or floor panels
not_for: devices on concrete or masonry without framing (use slab sleeve / chase rules)
deciding code compliance (the code checks still apply)
packs.rule: Place every device the way the panel manufacturer would build it: the framing is part of the layout from the first preview, not a correction at rough-in. 1) Build the layout preview on top of the framing layout (studs, plates, headers, rafters or joists, blocking, sheathing joints), not on the room outline alone. 2) Walls: box beside a stud, never on it (single-gang centre 47 mm from the stud axis, 2-gang and round boxes 75 mm), on the side that keeps the cavity widest; keep clear of corner and king/jack studs, headers, plates and sheathing joints; one standard height per device type (receptacles 300 mm, counter 1,100 mm, switches 1,220 mm) unless the code or the owner says otherwise. 3) Roofs and ceilings: devices centred in the rafter or joist bay where the room allows; minimum clearance 19 mm + device radius + 10 mm from the member axis; driver and junction boxes inside the same bay. 4) Floors: floor boxes, registers and drains in the joist bay (or in planned slab sleeves), never through a joist or beam. 5) Prefer devices on prefab panels in bays that are open in the factory; group devices so one bay or one wire run serves several. 6) After moving a device for the framing, re-run the code checks (NEC spacing) before modelling.
validation: Every wall box ≥ required distance from every stud axis (report the minimum)
Every ceiling device ≥ clearance from every rafter or joist axis and inside its room
NEC spacing checks still pass after framing moves
Rough-in clash check: only soft layers cut

packs.title: Slab on grade from the framing layout (anchors, recess, stub-ups)

environment.tool: RevitBridge 0.4.0 with run_csharp

use_when: a prefab timber building sits on a slab on grade
anchor bolts, slab recesses or plumbing stub-ups must match wall panels and fixtures
not_for: structural design of the slab or anchorage (engineer of record)
raised floors on piers or ground screws
packs.rule: 1) Take the slab edge from the framing outer faces and the anchor lines from the bottom-plate segments of the current wall panels; at door openings there is no plate and no anchor. 2) Place anchors per plate segment: max spacing and end distance from the engineer (assumed 1219 / 305 mm), at least two per segment, clear of stud axes. 3) Keep stub-ups out of the thickened edge and record them from one slab corner. 4) A curbless shower is a slab recess with the full slab thickness below it; subtract it from the edge beam where they meet. 5) Show the 2D layout and BOM for review, then model it as one assembly (slab floor, recess floor, edge as Structural Foundation DirectShape, bolts, stub-ups) and clash-check it against the wall assemblies: bolts through bottom plates are intended. 6) Re-derive the anchors whenever a wall panel is rebuilt.
validation: Anchor report per plate segment: count, max gap, end distances, min distance to a stud axis
Stub-ups outside the thickened edge (except where intended)
Clash check against wall assemblies: only bolt x bottom plate / insulation
Placeholder host dependents checked before deletion

packs.title: Sloped roof assembly from component families

environment.tool: RevitBridge 0.4.0 (local Revit API bridge, MCP) with run_csharp

use_when: framing and finishing a sloped (shed, mono-pitch) roof as an assembly of lumber, sheet and board families
placing sheet goods, insulation or trim on a sloped plane
covering rafter tails and fly rafters with fascia and barge boards
not_for: prefabricated trusses modelled as single families
curved roofs
packs.rule: 1) Check family placement type before reuse; make work-plane-based copies under new names. 2) Flex-test the plane orientation (cut vector sign) with one instance and read back the transform. 3) Compute every sloped member from one layout rule; offset square-cut ends by depth x sin(slope); members that carry the deck (outlookers, flat blocking) are rotated to the slope (cross-section rotation = slope angle; check the sign by the top-face normal), with their top on the rafter-top plane. 4) Dry-run the whole build with an all-pairs clash check and commit only when every remaining contact is on an allow-list of intended conditions. 5) Verify that trim covers every exposed cut by comparing end-face extents with trim extents. 6) Before documenting, check every modelled piece against its stock size (no piece longer than the sheet or board it is cut from). 7) After Duplicate(), reset Cost, Type Comments and other data parameters of every new type; duplicated types inherit them silently. 8) Insulation (batts, foam) runs only inside the exterior wall lines, bearing to bearing; eaves and rake overhangs are not insulated. 9) Walls are built to fit the roof, as a prefab plant would: no wedge or pony wall. The high wall is framed taller (cap at the rafter bearing), the end walls are raked (sloped double top plate, studs cut to it), and sheathing, insulation and siding are cut to the rafter line inside the wall panels. The roof assembly holds only roof components. The design (host) walls follow the roof too: sloped wall profile on the raked walls, raised top on the high wall; the wall gypsum stops under the ceiling drywall (rafter line minus the drywall thickness), so the ceiling board runs over the wall top. 10) Before changing the members of an assembly instance, check whether its type is shared by other instances; if so, build a new assembly (AssemblyInstance.Create) instead, because Revit asks a modal question no script can answer and then copies the change to every instance (FP15). Box families cannot make sloped edges: use DirectShape extrusions with material and Comments/Mark for the BOM.
validation: Flex test transform equals expected axes
Clash check: only allow-listed contacts
End faces of all rafters, fly rafters and outlookers inside fascia/barge extents
Assembly member count equals pieces built
No piece longer than its stock length
Every type in the assembly has its own Cost and unit in Type Comments
Insulation bounding box inside the outer face of the wall framing (ADU-01: batts y -1134.1..2456.2 within -1172.7..2494.8; x -3944.9..8002.7 within -3983..8040.8)
Top-face normal of every deck-bearing member equals the roof normal
Every exterior face below the roof is closed: framing, insulation, sheathing, siding and gypsum reach the rafter line on all walls

inputs.ALLOW: intended contacts, 'Kind A x Kind B'

packs.title: Residential branch circuits from a confirmed layout

environment.tool: RevitBridge 0.4.0 with run_csharp

use_when: electrical for a small dwelling unit or ADU: panel, receptacles, lighting, smoke alarms, circuits
placing wall and ceiling devices by API on host-wall faces and ceiling planes
creating circuits and a panel schedule by API
not_for: commercial distribution or three-phase systems
load calculations or code compliance sign-off (electrical engineer / AHJ)
conduit or cable routing
packs.rule: 1) Lay out devices in 2D first, on top of the framing layout (ARPL-ASM-0007), and check them against NEC 210.52 (wall spacing 1.83 m, counter 600 mm, bath basin 900 mm, front/back exterior, HVAC service receptacle 7.5 m) before modelling; the owner confirms. 2) Check what content exists; author missing families from Family Templates with PowerBalanced connectors (ARPL-CON-0001); wall-mounted ones from 'Electrical Fixture.rft' (switch category if needed), not from 'Lighting Fixture.rft'. 3) Place wall devices on host-wall side faces, fetching fresh face references for every placement (FP18); ceiling devices on a horizontal reference plane at the finished ceiling. 4) Before circuiting, probe the panel's supply connector (voltage, poles) against the distribution system; template commercial panelboards are 208 V 3-pole. Probe device loads (some types carry 0 VA). 5) Create circuits in the order of the planned numbering; for loads above 80 % of the default 20 A rating expect a modal warning during ElectricalSystem.Create (FP17): watch the screen, or create them with a temporary small load. 6) Place the panel schedule, export the sheet as an image and look at it; sync after the checks pass. 7) Before rough-in, check every device against the framing: wall box centre ≥ 19 + half box width + 3 mm from a stud axis (47 mm single-gang, 75 mm round 4 in), ceiling device ≥ 19 + radius + 10 mm from a rafter axis and inside its room; move the device, then re-run the NEC spacing check. 8) Model the rough-in as members of the prefab assemblies (boxes, cut-outs, sleeves, nipples) and clash-check them: only insulation, sheathing, siding and drywall may be cut, never framing. Partition walls built on site get no rough-in pieces. 9) Re-run the wall-space check whenever doors or windows change: fixed panels of sliding glass doors count as wall space and the operable panels are doorways, so posts between standard sliders usually need their own receptacle. A wall panel rebuild deletes the rough-in in that assembly; re-run it for that wall only.
validation: NEC 210.52 spacing checks pass on the 2D layout
Every device placed within 2 mm of its face (report distance)
Panel connector voltage/poles match the distribution system
Circuit numbers equal the planned numbers; ratings and loads read back
Panel schedule and sheet exported and inspected
Rough-in clash check: only soft layers cut (XPS, plywood, siding, drywall, batt)
Wall-space check re-run after every opening change

packs.title: Weekly clash run inside Revit by solid intersection across open cloud models; penetrations separated, clashes grouped, owner by routing priority

environment.tool: RevitBridge MCP with run_csharp
environment.model: Autodesk sample Snowdon Towers, 6 cloud discipline models; 9 pairs

use_when: A federated project needs a weekly clash number per discipline pair and the cloud project has no clash service (no Model Coordination module)
Clash results must carry element unique ids so next week's run can report new and resolved clashes
A quick hard-clash check before publishing models for formal coordination
not_for: Clearance (soft) clashes: needs inflated solids, not recorded yet
Walls and floors against services when the service openings are not modelled: every crossing would count
Models that do not share one internal origin and shared position: transform one side by the link transform first
Replacing a coordination service where one is available: use its tracked clash groups instead
packs.rule:
1. Agree the clash matrix with the team first: category pairs, hard or clearance, routing priority (who moves).
2. Open every model in one session with link worksets closed; check that all report the same shared position (ProjectLocation.GetProjectPosition at the origin) and that link transforms are identity. Otherwise transform the second model's solids by the link transform.
3. Per pair: bounding-box prefilter, then BooleanOperationsUtils intersection; count a clash when the intersection volume exceeds a small threshold (0.0001 cf used). Cache solids; walk GeometryInstance with GetInstanceGeometry.
4. Write one row per element pair: both unique ids and element ids, categories, family and type, levels, volume, centroid. Keep it under the bridge's reply limit by splitting pairs across calls and appending to a run log; on a timeout read the log, never rerun blindly.
5. Classify: vertical runs through ceilings (and later through walls or floors with modelled openings) are penetrations, reported separately.
6. Group clashes that share an element (union-find); report groups, not only clashes. Owner by routing priority.
7. Close the opened models without saving (Document.Close(false)); they were only read.
8. Next week: match by the pair of unique ids to report new, resolved and still open.
validation: Every model reports the same shared position; every link transform is identity (or the transform was applied).
Run log lists every pair of the agreed matrix with a count and duration.
Penetrations + clashes = raw intersections; each clash has a group and an owner.
Opened models closed unchanged (no sync).

packs.title: Shop drawings: invalid references and swapped elevations

environment.tool: RevitBridge 0.4.0 (local Revit API bridge, MCP) with run_csharp

use_when: creating dimensioned shop drawings or assembly sheets
adding many dimensions by script
packs.rule: Isolate risky annotation in its own transaction and verify every sheet visually. Regenerate the shop drawing whenever the assembly members are replaced: dimensions reference member faces and are deleted with them. DirectShape faces take dimension references like family geometry. Sloped faces cannot be dimensioned in an elevation chain; state the heights at both ends in a note on the view. Check the assembly frame first (FP16). When rescaling: crop plans to the building first (clear scope boxes, which override the crop), turn on annotation crop, trim section width and far clip, hide markers that a template will not let you hide by category (HideElements), then re-pack sheets and check every viewport against the drawing area. A single-view sheet is centred, never emptied; continuation sheets (<number>A) only for real overflow on multi-view sheets (FP23).

Every viewport inside the title block drawing area and no overlaps after a scale change

packs.title: Weekly print-set booklets with ZEN: one Revit print set per model, Print Intel workbook, ACC Gate Print PDFs

environment.tool: RevitBridge MCP with run_csharp, plus desktop control for Revit and ZEN dialogs
environment.batch_tool: ZEN 1.2 (Revit add-in by Tiverit LLC): Export Print Intel, Print PDF, ACC Gate
environment.model: 6-model Snowdon Towers sample (Autodesk), workshared ACC cloud models

use_when: A federated project needs one PDF booklet per model every week without opening the models by hand
The ZEN add-in (Tiverit LLC) is installed and the project has a ZEN model registry of ACC cloud models
An agent prepares print sets in Revit and drives ZEN Print Intel and ACC Gate from a bridge with screen access
not_for: Projects without ZEN: export PDFs per model from the bridge with PDFExportOptions instead (same content rule, same read-back)
Sets that must follow the sheet list automatically: a Revit print set is a fixed list (see rule 9)
packs.rule:
1. The print set is a Revit print set (ViewSheetSet), one per model, with the same name in every model (for example <Project>-current). ZEN does not create it: Export Print Intel reads the model's print sets into the workbook, and Print PDF and ACC Gate print the workbook's PrintJobs rows.
2. Decide the content before creating anything, with the read-only check (final/checks/printset_readback.cs, before creation it lists the content): a sheet belongs in the set when it carries a viewport, a schedule (ScheduleSheetInstance other than the title-block revision schedule) or a panel schedule (PanelScheduleSheetInstance). Ask the user whether schedule-only sheets count; show the skipped sheets.
3. Create it in Revit: Print (Ctrl+P) > Selected views/sheets > Select. If an existing set already holds exactly the listed sheets, select it and use the 'Save as' icon (top right) with the common name. Otherwise Save as first, then Check none, untick 'Hide un-checked views/sheets', type 'Sheet:' in the filter and tick the listed sheets. Then Save current set, Select, and close the Print dialog with Close, never OK. The link 'Create a print set' only opens online help.
4. Read back with the check: set exists, would_add 0, would_remove 0, no non-sheet views. Only then synchronize with central with a comment and relinquish: ACC Gate opens the central model, and an unsynced set does not exist there.
5. Export Print Intel (ZEN > Data & Health > Print PDF split button, id CustomCtrl_%CustomCtrl_%CustomCtrl_%ZEN%Data & Health%ZenPrintPdf%CmdExportPrintIntelWorkbook) into one workbook folder per project. Check the PrintSets sheet lists the set with the expected sheet count and ModelInfo carries the cloud GUIDs (ACC Gate matches by GUID). The export overwrites an existing workbook without asking; its folder browser starts at Desktop.
6. Fill PrintJobs: one row per PDF, PrintSetName copied exactly from PrintSets, PdfSetupName blank for ZEN's default profile (each sheet at its own size, vector, colour, sheet-number order), BaseFileName optional (default <Model>_<Set>). Save and close the workbook before the run.
7. Weekly run: ACC Gate with no model open: registry CSV, all models, action 'Print PDFs from Print Intel workbooks', the workbook folder, and the output folder typed as <workbook folder>/<date> (FP51). A command posted while Revit Home is showing waits until Home is left (FP53): leave Home with the back arrow, or click the ribbon button, and take a screenshot after posting.
8. Check the output: one PDF per model in PDF/, page count equal to the set's sheet count in the workbook, every sheet number present, batch report without failures.
9. A Revit print set is a fixed list: a sheet added later is missed and a sheet emptied later stays in. Run the check weekly as a drift check and update the set (step 3) when would_add or would_remove is not 0.
10. Links unloaded in a model stay unloaded and do not print (ZEN manual); the workbook's Links sheet shows IsLoaded as of the export session. Confirm linked content on one site or overall sheet in the PDF.
11. Bridge mechanics: open each model with OpenAndActivateDocument from the registry GUIDs (worksets closed) and work on uiapp.ActiveUIDocument.Document; close the previous model by the reference captured before opening, never the document the bridge passes as doc; close the active model with PostableCommand.Close (FP54).
validation: Read-back check pass in every model (would_add 0, would_remove 0, non_sheet_views 0)
Every workbook: PrintSets lists the set with the expected sheet count; PrintJobs has the set name; ModelInfo has the model's cloud GUIDs
One PDF per model; page count equal to the set's sheet count; every sheet number present
Batch report and run log without failures

packs.title: Governed material Descriptions and Keynotes

environment.tool: Revit material export to CSV, AI proposal reviewed in Excel, re-import into Revit
environment.review: adversarial rule review by a second model (Mistral)

use_when: A Revit material schedule contains blank, incomplete or contradictory Description values.
Materials need Keynote values for material tags or sheet keynote legends.
Material data is exported to CSV, AI-reviewed and read back into Revit.
A Revit Bridge reads material properties, requests an AI proposal, previews the proposal and commits approved changes.
not_for: Inventing manufacturer, product, grade, performance or specification properties that are not supported by the source data.
Replacing an approved office or project keynote database without explicit authorization.
Treating appearance assets as authoritative physical specifications.
Automatically describing analytical, phase, poche, default or other graphic/system materials as construction materials unless the user explicitly wants them documented.
Merging, deduplicating, renaming or deleting Revit materials as a side effect of metadata enrichment.
packs.rule:
0. ACTORS AND AUTHORITY
Use three explicit actors:
- AI: interprets evidence and proposes changes. AI never performs an uncontrolled production write.
- Approver: human or pre-authorized policy that accepts, rejects, quarantines or escalates a proposal.
- Engine: performs only approved deterministic writes and verifies the result.

1. PRESERVE THE ROUND-TRIP SCHEMA
When editing an exported material CSV intended for Revit re-import, the Engine must not add, remove, rename or reorder columns. It must not rename materials. It may modify only fields explicitly authorized by the workflow, normally Description and/or Keynote. Metadata enrichment must not merge, deduplicate or delete materials.

2. CLASSIFY BEFORE ENRICHING
The AI must first classify each row as one of:
PHYSICAL | FINISH | SYSTEM | GRAPHIC | ANALYTICAL | UNKNOWN.

Classification is part of the proposal and must include evidence.
Useful deterministic hints include Revit class/category metadata and name patterns such as Default, Poche, Analytical, Phase -, Clearance and similar system/graphic terms. Name-pattern hints are evidence, not sole authority.
SYSTEM, GRAPHIC and ANALYTICAL rows must not receive invented construction descriptions or classification keynotes unless the Approver explicitly authorizes a separate internal documentation namespace.
UNKNOWN must be reviewed rather than silently promoted to PHYSICAL.

3. MATERIAL DESCRIPTION GRAMMAR
For PHYSICAL or FINISH materials, the AI may propose Description from supported evidence in this order:
Base Material -> Product/Form -> Finish/Treatment -> Color -> Pattern/Texture -> Grade/Performance.
Omit any component that is not supported.

Description describes what the material is and how it is finished. It does not describe its instance size or type dimensions.

Hard exclusions from Description:
- dimensions, thicknesses and sizes;
- model/type numbers unless they are part of the actual product identity explicitly required by the Approver;
- project codes;
- keynote numbers;
- unsupported manufacturer/product claims;
- completion-looking placeholders such as N/A, Unknown, TBD, To Be Determined or equivalent, unless the governing standard explicitly requires that literal value.

4. EVIDENCE AUTHORITY
Use Name and Class primarily for material identity.
Use an existing Description as evidence, but test it for contradictions.
Use explicit terms in Name as strong evidence.
Use Appearance Asset and appearance properties as visual evidence for attributes such as color, gloss, texture and transparency.
Do not promote an appearance texture or asset name into a physical/specification claim unless corroborated.
Appearance-only color is low-confidence visual evidence: the AI may propose it, but the Engine must not commit it into Description unless corroborated or specifically approved.
Use Keynote only as a classification hint, not as proof of physical properties.

5. CONFLICT HANDLING
If Name, Description, Class and Appearance conflict, the AI must not silently merge contradictory claims. It must record the conflict in the proposal and prefer explicit material identity over purely visual appearance.
The AI may mark an unambiguous correction as high confidence, but it does not directly commit it.
The Engine may commit only after the Approver or a documented pre-authorized approval policy permits that specific change class.

6. KEYNOTE AUTHORITY AND STATES
If an approved office/project keynote table exists, it is the governing authority.

Define keynote state as:
- VALID: key exists in the governing table and resolves to the expected entry.
- SUSPICIOUS: key exists and resolves, but conflicts with the material evidence, approved mapping or intended documentation use. Preserve it, quarantine/flag it, and do not silently replace it.
- INVALID: key is absent from the governing table or fails resolution.

The Engine must preserve existing VALID keynotes unless remapping is explicitly authorized.
The AI may flag SUSPICIOUS or INVALID keynotes but may not overwrite them without approval.
Never invent a new key because a classification number merely looks plausible.
If no reliable approved match exists, leave Keynote blank or route to review.

Match priority:
a. exact approved material/library match;
b. equivalent approved material family ONLY when equivalence is defined by a documented approved mapping table or library relationship;
c. approved keynote database/table match;
d. approved specification/classification mapping;
e. no match -> review/blank.

7. GENERATING A NEW PROJECT KEYNOTE SET
Only generate new material keynotes when the Approver explicitly requests creation of a new project keynote system and no governing table must be preserved.
Use:
<approved classification section>.<local family letter><variant number>

The classification section is the authoritative classification anchor.
The suffix is local project/office syntax, not an official meaning supplied by the classification standard.
The family letter groups related materials within a section.
The number distinguishes documented material variants.

For material-tag and sheet-legend workflows, default to a unique suffix when two variants must appear as separate legend entries. Variants may share a key only when they are intentionally represented by the same legend/specification entry.

A generated keynote is not complete until a matching keynote text-table entry exists and resolves correctly in Revit.

8. AI PROPOSAL SIDECAR
AI reasoning and review metadata must live outside the Revit round-trip CSV unless the governing schema explicitly provides fields for them.
Use a sidecar proposal record with at least:
{
  "material": "<existing material name>",
  "classification": "PHYSICAL|FINISH|SYSTEM|GRAPHIC|ANALYTICAL|UNKNOWN",
  "proposed_description": "<string|null>",
  "proposed_keynote": "<string|null>",
  "keynote_state": "VALID|SUSPICIOUS|INVALID|null",
  "evidence": ["<source/value/reason>"],
  "conflicts": ["<conflict>"],
  "confidence": 0.0,
  "decision": "PROPOSE|REVIEW|QUARANTINE|NO_CHANGE"
}

The sidecar is advisory/audit data. The Engine writes only approved production values into the authoritative CSV/Revit model.

9. COMMIT
CSV workflow:
Revit export -> AI sidecar proposal -> Approver/policy decision -> Engine edits only authorized existing cells -> Revit import -> read-back verification.

Bridge workflow:
Read Material -> gather governed evidence -> AI sidecar proposal -> preview/dry run -> Approver/policy decision -> approved ExternalEvent -> Transaction -> set authorized values -> regenerate/read back -> verify.

10. REVIT API WRITE AND RESOLUTION CHECKS
Do not assume that the existence of BuiltInParameter.KEYNOTE_PARAM guarantees a writable Material keynote in every target version/document.
For Revit 2024-2027, the Engine must runtime-check that the target Material exposes the expected keynote parameter, that it is writable when a write is requested, and that the storage/value behavior is as expected before calling Parameter.Set.
Use the governing KeynoteTable/KeynoteEntry data where available to validate membership and resolution.
If parameter access, writability or keynote-table resolution differs from expectation, do not substitute a guessed API path or value; flag the material/workflow for review.

11. FAIL SAFE
When evidence is insufficient, omit the unsupported Description component or leave Keynote blank.
Do not pad missing information with placeholders that merely make the record look complete.
Missing data is preferable to plausible invented BIM data.
validation: CSV validation:
row count unchanged;
column count, names and order unchanged;
material Name unchanged;
no materials merged, deduplicated or deleted;
every non-authorized cell byte/value-equivalent to the source;
Description contains no copied dimensions/sizes;
Description contains no banned completion placeholder unless explicitly required;
no unsupported physical claim was introduced;
existing VALID Keynotes remain unchanged unless remapping was authorized.
Proposal/sidecar validation:
every record identifies the existing material name;
classification is one of the allowed states;
evidence is present for every proposed non-null Description or Keynote;
conflicts are surfaced, not silently resolved;
appearance-only color is marked as low-confidence evidence unless corroborated;
UNKNOWN classification cannot auto-commit;
SUSPICIOUS or INVALID keynote state cannot auto-commit;
equivalent-family matching cites an approved mapping relationship.
Keynote validation:
VALID means both governing-table membership and successful resolution;

every selected approved key exists in the governing keynote table and resolves to the expected entry; or, for a newly authorized project keynote set, every generated key has a corresponding text-table entry;
no single key resolves to conflicting legend text;
distinct material variants receive distinct keys when the intended sheet legend requires separate entries;
suffix semantics are documented as local, not represented as official classification semantics.
Revit/API validation:
before write, confirm the target Material exposes the expected keynote parameter and that it is writable for the requested operation;
commit occurs inside the required Revit API transaction path;
read back Description and Keynote after commit;
confirm the material tag reports the expected keynote;
place or refresh a keynote legend and confirm key and text resolve as intended;
if read-back, parameter access or legend resolution differs from the approved proposal, roll back where possible or quarantine/flag the material for review.

Defence: unattended bridges must register a failure preprocessor (IFailuresPreprocessor) and a DialogBoxShowing handler before the first batch write, or a single warning freezes the run.

failure_patterns.meaning: The correction addressed one case of the problem; the same problem reappeared in a neighbouring case.

failure_patterns.name: Frame chosen from a name
failure_patterns.meaning: The agent picks the domain, discipline or meaning of a task from a familiar word (a name, an acronym, 'connector', 'panel', 'room', 'system') before inspecting the actual evidence, then executes valid operations in the wrong world. Rule: Identify -> Inspect -> Frame -> Act, not Recognize -> Assume -> Act.

failure_patterns.name: Exception leaves a transaction open
failure_patterns.meaning: A scripted error escapes while the script's own Transaction is still open. Inside an enclosing TransactionGroup this can crash Revit (fatal error) instead of failing the script. Defence: using-blocks for every Transaction, try/catch around the body, dry runs. See FP28: the using-block pattern is the defence, and also the trap when Commit is never reached.
failure_patterns.found_by: Revit journal after a fatal error

evidence.note: Arnost Lobel's transaction advice series: scope transactions in using-blocks (which automagically dispose and roll back), check transaction status, and handle transaction groups deliberately - the foundation of the FP14 defence.

failure_patterns.name: Shared assembly type edited through one instance
failure_patterns.meaning: Adding or removing members of an AssemblyInstance whose AssemblyType is used by other instances makes Revit ask (modal dialog, not a failure message) whether to update the type. The failures preprocessor cannot answer it, the API call blocks until a person does, and the change may be copied to every instance (members duplicated over the other instances). Defence: before editing members, count instances of the type; if more than one, create a new assembly from the new members instead and delete the old instance with its members.
failure_patterns.found_by: Bridge timeout; owner at the Revit dialog

failure_patterns.name: New assembly frame follows the project axes
failure_patterns.meaning: AssemblyInstance.Create gives the assembly a transform along the project X/Y axes, not along the element it describes. Assembly views (CreateDetailSection elevations, plan sections) and any dimensions computed in the assembly frame then look at the wrong side or collapse to one segment. Defence: after creating an assembly for a wall panel, call SetTransform so BasisX runs along the wall and BasisY points to the interior, before creating its views.

failure_patterns.name: Modal warning raised inside an API call
failure_patterns.meaning: Some Revit API calls post a warning as a modal dialog during the call itself, before the script can change the condition (ElectricalSystem.Create checks the load against the default 20 A rating). The transaction's failures preprocessor does not see it; the bridge call blocks until a person answers. Defence: anticipate the condition (temporary small load, set limits first), and when a bridge call times out, look at the screen before anything else.

failure_patterns.name: Stale geometry references after regeneration
failure_patterns.meaning: Face references collected before other elements were placed on the same host can be invalid after a regeneration; using them for face-based placement throws a native SEHException instead of a managed error. Defence: fetch the host's face references immediately before each placement.

failure_patterns.name: Unknown tool parameter silently ignored
failure_patterns.meaning: A misspelled or unsupported parameter (here mode instead of transaction) is dropped without an error, so the call runs with defaults: scripts that start their own Transaction fail inside the default wrapper. failure_patterns.name: Application reminder dialog blocks an automated run
failure_patterns.meaning: Revit's periodic "Changes Not Synchronized with Central" reminder is modal and stops a running command past the bridge timeout; a partial run can leave half-finished state (old views deleted, new ones not yet created). failure_patterns.name: Read-only collection returned by the API

failure_patterns.name: Long export outlives the call timeout
failure_patterns.meaning: A combined PDF export of 14+ sheets takes over 60 s; the bridge call times out while Revit keeps exporting. Defence: watch the status bar until it reads Ready, then check the file size and time before the next command.
failure_patterns.found_by: status bar progress in a screenshot

evidence.note: Not only exports: a single run_csharp write call creating levels, slabs, columns and walls outlived the 60 s bridge timeout, and a read-only follow-up timed out too, while Revit had committed everything. Re-running would have duplicated every element. Defence: keep each write stage well inside the timeout, never retry a write after a timeout, and query the model by Mark before deciding (ARPL-GEO-0004).

Cloud operations too: SaveAsCloudModel plus EnableCloudWorksharing took 60-90 s and outlived the bridge reply every time; during 'Enable Worksharing' further calls also timed out. The model was uploaded each time. Defence: one long call per model, then wait and read IsModelInCloud / IsWorkshared / the cloud model GUID in a short call; never resend (ARPL-ADM-0003).

failure_patterns.name: Viewport outline inflated by elements outside the crop
failure_patterns.meaning: Section marks, camera markers and similar elements beyond the crop region set the viewport outline, so a rescaled view looks too big for its sheet; an automatic packer then moves it away. Defence: crop and annotation-crop first, find elements whose view bounding box extends past the crop, trim or hide them, and never empty a single-view sheet.

failure_patterns.name: Local cloud cache exhausts the disk during a batch run
failure_patterns.meaning: Every cloud model opened or synced is copied into the local collaboration cache (CollaborationCache under %LOCALAPPDATA%\Autodesk\Revit\<version>). A batch over many models can fill the drive mid-run; Revit then fails saves or syncs in ways that look like model or network errors. Defence: check free space before a batch (several GB per dozen models), and let the user clear the cache with Revit closed; never delete it from a running session.

failure_patterns.name: Dependency inferred from a message string
failure_patterns.meaning: A help text, dialog message or log line names features that need a credential, licence or service, and the agent repeats it as fact. Such strings are often older than the code. Defence: confirm a dependency from the behaviour (does the command run without it?) or from the code path, and name the source when reporting it.

failure_patterns.name: Internal database units assumed
failure_patterns.meaning: The Revit API returns and expects raw database units; length is feet and area is square feet, regardless of the project's display units. A '200 mm' wall reads as 0.656 in the API. An agent that writes millimetre or metre values into geometry calls produces a model wrong by a factor of 304.8 or 3.28 - with no error, no warning, no failed call. Defence: Treat every raw API length as feet and every area as square feet. Never mix project display units into geometry calls. Convert explicitly (UnitUtils, or the 0.3048 factor) only at display and export boundaries. Sanity-check one known dimension against the UI before any batch write.

failure_patterns.name: Stale geometry read after modify
failure_patterns.meaning: After changing an element (parameter, location, type), geometry queried before regeneration or commit reflects the old state. In batch workflows and manual regeneration mode this becomes systematic: the agent measures and validates against yesterday's model. Source quote: 'The only problem is the risk of missing a regeneration and retrieving stale data.' Defence: Modify, then regenerate (or commit), then measure. Never read geometry to validate a change made in the same unregenerated pass. Regenerating more often than necessary is cheap; a stale read is invisible. After any write through a bridge, force a refresh (RefreshActiveView / UpdateAllOpenViews where available) before any verification pass, in addition to regenerate-then-read.

failure_patterns.name: Uncommitted transaction rolls back silently
failure_patterns.meaning: A Transaction in a using-block that never reaches Commit() disposes and rolls back with no exception: the code appears to succeed and the model is unchanged. The opposite face (an exception escaping with an open transaction crashing Revit inside a TransactionGroup) is already FP14; this entry adds the silent-rollback side, which is the one an agent cannot notice from the return values alone. Defence: Commit explicitly inside the using block, check the returned TransactionStatus, and treat RollBack-on-dispose as a failure path, not a default. Wrap the body in try/catch so no exception escapes with the transaction open. After any batch: read back a sample of changes to confirm they exist. For agent workflows spanning multiple tool calls, request a TransactionGroup wrapper so the run is atomic and undoable as one unit; keep read-back verification after every batch regardless.

failure_patterns.name: API call outside valid Revit context
failure_patterns.meaning: Revit API calls are valid only inside an API context (external command, ExternalEvent). Called from background threads, timers or modeless dialogs they fail unpredictably: a transaction 'refuses to start for no apparent reason', a call that worked before fails 'except for the exact time', sometimes Revit records errors only in the journal or crashes. Intermittent, non-reproducible failures are the signature. Defence: Never call the Revit API from a thread or UI callback. Marshal every request through a raised ExternalEvent and keep Idling as a last resort. If an API call fails intermittently with no code change, suspect the calling context before the call. Treat a timeout as 'state unknown', not 'call failed': never blindly re-issue an identical write (double-apply risk); check for a blocking dialog, a busy Revit, or a dead ExternalEvent first, and make write retries idempotent.

Every model edit goes through an ExternalEvent raised from the handler and executed later in a valid, writable context.

failure_patterns.name: Name-based parameter lookup ambiguity
failure_patterns.meaning: Name-based parameter lookups return the first match and null on no match. With shared and project parameter name collisions, or family versus type parameters, an agent silently reads or writes the wrong parameter, or dereferences null and the run dies mid-batch. Defence: Prefer BuiltInParameter or parameter GUID lookups. Null-check every parameter before use. When only a name is available, verify the result (owning element, definition, storage type) before reading or writing. Treat a duplicate name as an error, not a first-match windfall.

failure_patterns.name: Posted command assumed immediate

Defence: Treat a posted command as fire-and-forget: schedule any follow-up work in an ExternalEvent, and never read model state in the same call sequence assuming the posted command already ran.

failure_patterns.name: Dry-run transaction group assimilated instead of rolled back

After the group ends, read back a sample before the next step to confirm the document is in the expected state.

failure_patterns.name: Advertised tool contract desync
failure_patterns.meaning: The bridge's advertised contract and its actual behaviour disagree, in two documented faces. (a) Registry desync: tools/list advertises tools the Revit side never registered. Agents call them and get 'Method not found' while every genuinely registered tool works; root-caused in the archived revit-mcp as implemented C# commands missing from the plugin's command manifest, so they were implemented but undiscoverable. An agent in this state burned multiple turns rotating through ai_element_filter, get_current_view_elements, send_code_to_revit and get_available_family_types, all listed, all 'not found', on two machines and two Revit versions. (b) Schema desync: a tool's JSON schema advertises null as the default for optional arguments, but the validator rejects null when a client actually sends it. Agent frameworks that fill every optional field from the schema get validation errors on tools that would have run had the field been omitted. Defence: Treat tools/list and tool schemas as unverified advertisement, not ground truth. On 'Method not found' or an argument-validation error on an advertised tool, do not rewrite the request: probe a known-good cheap tool to separate channel faults from contract faults, then degrade to the tools that verifiably respond, and report the desync instead of iterating. When composing parallel plans, fill only arguments with real values and omit optionals rather than sending advertised defaults.

failure_patterns.name: Parallel tool calls share one handler (false success, wrong data)
failure_patterns.meaning: Bridges built on a single module-level request handler / ExternalEvent cannot serve concurrent requests. When an MCP client (which issues tool calls in parallel by default) sends overlapping API-context calls, only some handlers execute, and every waiting caller receives the same response, all with HTTP 200. Model edits are skipped while their callers are told they succeeded, and follow-up requests are answered with the previous request's response until the server idles. No exception, no log entry: in the documented repro, six concurrent calls each received one handler's answer, only two of six handlers ran, and four model edits were skipped while reported as successful. Root-caused upstream in pyRevit Routes (one shared handler per request thread), fixed upstream, but the agent-facing fault class generalises to any single-threaded host bridge. Defence: Never issue concurrent API-context tool calls; serialise all tool traffic to one Revit session. Treat HTTP 200 as unproven: after any write, read back the changed state before declaring success. If a bridge is known to serialise internally, still verify writes, because residual races remain (two server processes on one Revit, or a client-side timeout while the call still executes inside Revit, which re-applies on retry).

failure_patterns.name: Bridge rejects or drops a valid request (channel faults that blame the caller)
failure_patterns.meaning: Transport- and protocol-level faults surface as errors that accuse the agent's request. A well-formed JSON-RPC body is answered with 'Invalid JSON' (-32700) because the plugin's embedded HTTP server omits the HTTP status line, so the response parses as HTTP/0.9. Node.js resolves 'localhost' to IPv6 ::1 while the Revit plugin listens on IPv4 only, so every tool call fails with ECONNREFUSED although the server is up and the requests are perfect. The agent's natural response — rewriting the payload, alternating encodings, retrying with variations — cannot succeed, and the transcript shows the agent unable to distinguish its own malformed request from a broken channel. Defence: On a transport or parse error, verify the channel before touching the payload: connect by explicit 127.0.0.1 rather than localhost, probe the port, call a known-good healthcheck tool. Never 'fix' a request that was well-formed; distinguish 'request invalid' from 'channel broken' before any retry; cap the retry loop and escalate rather than mutate.

failure_patterns.name: Name mangling across the serialization boundary
failure_patterns.meaning: Non-ASCII element names (Cyrillic, CJK, Arabic, umlauts, accents) are replaced with '?' by ASCII-fallback normalization on the bridge side. Listing tools return names like '????? 1'; the agent then sends the mangled name back into any lookup-by-name tool, and the lookup fails. The agent reads this as 'element not found' and iterates on the lookup, when the element exists and its name was destroyed in transit. Documented on a pyRevit/IronPython bridge where str vs unicode matters, with an independent fix in a community fork confirming the fault recurs across implementations. This is the string face of the class FP26 covers for numbers: values corrupted crossing the bridge boundary, invisibly, with the round-trip as the trap. Defence: Prefer ElementId over names as the round-trip key across any bridge. On first listing, test name integrity: fetch a name, query by it, and treat clusters of '?' or mojibake as a corruption signal, not as data. When a lookup fails for a name just returned by a listing tool, suspect boundary corruption before concluding the element is absent.

failure_patterns.name: Generated code compiled inside the host inherits an invisible environment
failure_patterns.meaning: Agent-authored C# sent to a code-execution tool is compiled by the bridge inside Revit, against an environment the agent cannot see. Three documented failure faces, one class: (a) the compiler adds every assembly loaded in the AppDomain as a metadata reference, so a third-party add-in with protected DLLs makes compilation fail before the agent's code is even parsed; (b) the bridge ships Roslyn with newer dependencies than the Revit release bundles, throwing a type-initializer exception on one Revit version while the identical call succeeds on the adjacent version; (c) Revit 2026 moved to .NET 8, which removed CodeDom compilation, so the legacy CSharpCodeProvider path throws 'Operation is not supported on this platform' — on Revit 2022 the same code ran. In all three faces the agent's code was correct, the compilation environment failed, and the transcripts show agents iterating on their own code, then falling back to manual instructions. Defence: After a compile failure of generated code, first compile a minimal known-good template. If the template fails, the environment is at fault: stop, report an environmental failure, and do not rewrite working code. Pin the compile target to the host's runtime (.NET Framework 4.8 vs .NET 8), expect platform shifts between Revit releases, and treat 'works on one release, fails on the neighbour' as an environment signature.

failure_patterns.name: Assumed execution-context variables in generated code
failure_patterns.meaning: Code-execution bridges inject the Revit context through template variables whose names are an unstated contract. The archived revit-mcp template exposed only lowercase 'document', while agents write 'Document' or 'doc' following the Dynamo and macro conventions, and expect 'uidoc' for selection work. The agent's code fails to access the current document although the document is passed to the executor, and the failure reads to the agent as a Revit API problem, or as its own hallucination — the reporter's own framing was 'wondering if this is a hallucination or fact?'. The fix was bridge-side aliases, confirming the contract, not the API, was at fault. The agent's own stack-trace diagnosis confidently blamed the wrong layer. Defence: Before writing real code against a code-execution tool, probe the execution contract: run a trivial template that returns the available context variables and their types. Never assume Dynamo or macro naming. On a 'variable not found' or 'cannot access document' error, print the available scope first and treat the template contract as the suspect, not the Revit API.

failure_patterns.name: API member assumed from another Revit version
failure_patterns.meaning: Generated code calls API members the agent remembers from another Revit release or from documentation, not from the installed API. In a Revit 2024 build, Wall.AddAttachment and AttachmentLocation did not exist, NonContinuousRailInfo had no public constructor, and a bridge helper name was guessed; each cost a compile round. Unlike FP38 the compile environment was fine: the agent's code was wrong. Defence: before using non-trivial members (wall attachment, rails, stairs, failure handling), reflect the installed types (GetMethods, GetConstructors) or compile a probe, and write against what exists. Revit 2024 equivalents found: profile walls instead of attachment (ARPL-GEO-0002); RailingType.RailStructure.AddNonContinuousRail(name, height, offset), then configure ProfileId; StairsEditScope.Commit with an IFailuresPreprocessor.
failure_patterns.found_by: Roslyn compile errors, resolved by reflecting the installed types

failure_patterns.name: Desktop action reaches the wrong window or instance
failure_patterns.meaning: Desktop-control actions act on whatever the operating system gives them, not on the model the agent means. Opening an application that is already running can start a second, empty instance instead of focusing the running one; typed text goes to whichever window has focus, for example the chat window that came to the front. Defence: never use open-application on a running Revit; prefer API routes (Document.ExportImage of a dedicated view) for visual checks; before typing into a dialog, click into its input field and confirm with a screenshot or zoom.
failure_patterns.found_by: screenshot showing a second Revit splash; bridge status listing two live sessions; a screenshot with the chat window in front of a file dialog
failure_patterns.revit_versions: observed in 2024; desktop layer, not the Revit API

failure_patterns.name: Null-conditional parameter write skips silently
failure_patterns.meaning: get_Parameter(...)?.Set(...) does nothing when the element has no such parameter, and the null-conditional hides it. 261 grids were 'tagged' with Comments, but grid datums have no ALL_MODEL_INSTANCE_COMMENTS, so no tag was written and a read-back found 0 grids. Defence: where a tag or value matters, fetch the parameter, fail loudly when it is null or read-only, and identify datums by a unique name prefix instead.

failure_patterns.name: Template placeholder taken as a real value
failure_patterns.meaning: Project templates ship with placeholder text in Project Information ('Building Name', 'Project Name'). The value is not empty, so tools that ask only for a missing value take the placeholder as real data: a model registry got 'Building Name' as a model key. Defence: before any step that reads identity fields, set them explicitly, and treat known placeholder strings as missing.
failure_patterns.found_by: reading the registry CSV
failure_patterns.revit_versions: any; template content

failure_patterns.name: Nearest-distance assignment misfiles elements
failure_patterns.meaning: Assigning elements to a building (or zone) by the nearest bounding box fails where buildings touch: a floor centre can be closer to the neighbour's box than to its own, so one building loses elements and its neighbour gains them. Defence: assign by containment in the owner's own extent (smallest containing extent wins), and check that per-group counts add up to the source total with nothing unassigned.
failure_patterns.found_by: per-file counts: one building with 0 floors, its neighbour with too many
failure_patterns.revit_versions: any; algorithmic

failure_patterns.name: Document state read from the path string
failure_patterns.meaning: After a failed or late-failing SaveAsCloudModel (name already exists), Document.PathName showed the cloud path although nothing had been saved: IsModelInCloud false, IsModified true, and EnableCloudWorksharing failed with 'does not have a central location'. An agent that judges success by PathName or by the title bar is wrong. Defence: read IsModelInCloud, IsWorkshared and GetCloudModelPath() (which throws for a non-cloud document).
failure_patterns.found_by: GetCloudModelPath threw 'not a cloud model' while PathName showed the cloud path

failure_patterns.name: Generated default contradicts the project setup
failure_patterns.meaning: A tool-generated configuration (here a host-by-link matrix exported from a registry) carries defaults that contradict decisions already made for the project: 'use shared coordinates' was false on every row of a federation built on shared coordinates. Run as generated, every link would have been placed origin to origin. Defence: before a batch run, read the generated configuration against the project's setup (coordinates, worksets, load behaviour) and change it on a backup copy.
failure_patterns.found_by: reading the matrix values before the run
failure_patterns.revit_versions: any; tool configuration

failure_patterns.name: Planned penetrations counted as clashes
failure_patterns.meaning: A geometric clash run reports every crossing, including services that are meant to pass through an element (a pipe dropping through a ceiling to a fixture, a duct through a wall with an opening still to come). Counted as clashes they bury the real conflicts and make the number meaningless. Defence: classify before reporting (direction of the run, modelled opening, category rule) and report penetrations separately; check fittings at those points by hand until they can be classified.
failure_patterns.found_by: reading the clash list by orientation of the running element
failure_patterns.revit_versions: any

failure_patterns.name: Expected cloud service missing from the project
failure_patterns.meaning: A workflow was planned around a cloud service (clash detection in ACC Model Coordination) that the project's subscription does not include; the project menu showed Data Management, Build, Design and admin modules only, and the product had been renamed (Autodesk Forma), so the expected entry was not where the instructions said. Defence: before planning on a cloud service, open the project's module list and confirm it; keep a bridge-based fallback (ARPL-CRD-0001).

failure_patterns.name: Completeness scored against an assumed requirement
failure_patterns.meaning: A fill-rate score is reported before the client's information requirement exists, with every schedule column assumed required. The number looks precise but measures the assumption: one optional field (Description) halved the score. Defence: print the assumption next to the number, and replace it with the client's LOIN table per category and stage as soon as it exists.
failure_patterns.found_by: comparing the score with what the client actually asked for
failure_patterns.revit_versions: any

failure_patterns.name: Batch report describes links as the batch opened them
failure_patterns.meaning: A batch tool opens each model with link worksets closed for speed; its health and placement reports then show every link as unloaded or in a closed workset, placement 'not checked', and instance names without the shared site. Read as project state, these would be false findings. Defence: treat link status and placement from such a batch as unknown; verify placement by link transform with links loaded, or run the report with links loaded.
failure_patterns.found_by: comparing the batch report with the same links loaded in one model
failure_patterns.revit_versions: any

failure_patterns.name: Dialog remembers another project's folder
failure_patterns.meaning: A batch dialog pre-fills the output folder last used, which belonged to another project; accepted, this week's outputs land in the wrong project's report folder and the report reads stale data. Defence: type the output folder (project and date) on every run and check where files were written.
failure_patterns.found_by: checking the output folder after the run
failure_patterns.revit_versions: any; tool dialog

failure_patterns.name: Panel schedule sheet read as empty
failure_patterns.meaning: A rule that decides sheet content from viewports and ScheduleSheetInstance misses panel schedules: on a sheet they are PanelScheduleSheetInstance, a separate class. Panel-schedule-only sheets are reported as empty and drop out of print sets, transmittals or sheet checks. Defence: count PanelScheduleSheetInstance with the schedules, and compare the result with the model's sheet list once.
failure_patterns.found_by: comparing a dry run with the electrical model's sheet list
failure_patterns.revit_versions: 2024; class unchanged since panel schedules were introduced

failure_patterns.name: Posted command waits on the Home screen
failure_patterns.meaning: With no model open and Revit Home showing, a command started by UIApplication.PostCommand (here an add-in batch command) returns 'posted' but does not run; it runs only when Home is left. An agent that waits for a dialog sees nothing and may post again. Defence: leave Home (back arrow) or click the ribbon button, and take a screenshot after posting before anything else.
failure_patterns.found_by: screenshots after posting the batch command

failure_patterns.name: Closing the document the bridge holds
failure_patterns.meaning: A bridge script passes one document as doc. Closing that document (for example in a loop over Application.Documents after opening the next model) throws InvalidObjectException, and the call reports an error although other documents in the loop did close. Defence: after OpenAndActivateDocument work on uiapp.ActiveUIDocument.Document, close only the previous model by the reference taken before opening, and close the active model with PostableCommand.Close; check the open documents after any error.
failure_patterns.found_by: state check after the error
